content: New health trends and innovations in service delivery, economic development, employment, migration, urbanization, conflict, environmental degradation, and technological advancements must all be taken into account when addressing health and well-being needs. For instance, an updated landscape analysis could uncover underutilized resources, such as the expansion of rural telecommunications infrastructure, which could be leveraged for telemedicine or the implementation of e-health and mobile health interventions. In humanitarian crises, countries or regions may need to urgently establish focused priorities for adolescent health and well-being. Conducting a situation analysis for adolescent sexual and reproductive health (SRH) in fragile settings is critical. For example, Sudan, where adolescents constitute about one-fourth of the population, recognized the need to address their diverse health needs. Despite having a national health plan, Sudan had not previously included adolescents, even though they represent a significant portion of the population with poor health outcomes. To address this, the Directorate of Maternal and Child Health of the Ministry of Health utilized the AA-HA. guidance to mobilize stakeholders and develop a National Strategy for Adolescent Health and Well-Being. This evidence-based approach engaged multiple government ministries, UN agencies, and civil society organizations to conduct a needs assessment, highlighting critical health needs for adolescents. Youth groups were actively involved to ensure their needs were understood and incorporated into the strategy. In Jamaica, significant progress has been made since the 1970s in reducing adolescent pregnancy rates and supporting pregnant adolescents. The adolescent fertility rate dropped from 157 births per 1,000 girls aged 15–19 in 1970 to 33 births per 1,000 in 2020. This success is partly attributed to innovative programs like the Programme for Adolescent Mothers (PAM), launched by the Women’s Centre of Jamaica Foundation. PAM encouraged pregnant adolescent girls to return to school after childbirth, provided education on sexuality to prevent repeat pregnancies, and built their self-confidence and life skills. The program, initially piloted in two centers, demonstrated promising results, with 73% of participants re-enrolling in secondary or vocational education and over 90% adopting contraception. These outcomes led to national scale-up, supported by government and partner funding, expanding to 10 centers and 8 outreach centers across Jamaica by 2018. Globally, the most impactful gains for adolescent well-being result from multisectoral action. Countries should invest in intersectoral programs for adolescent health and well-being to maximize the multiplier effect of coordinated efforts. School health programs, for example, are cost-effective and feasible in all settings, delivering significant benefits for human capital. Transitioning to health-promoting education systems that prioritize learners’ health and well-being as a core mission is essential. The WHO and UNESCO Global Standards for Health Promoting Schools provide a framework for adopting this holistic approach. Adolescent-responsive health systems are crucial for achieving universal health coverage (UHC). Establishing an adolescent health focal point within the Ministry of Health can ensure systematic attention to adolescent needs across all health programs and facilitate multisectoral collaboration. Adolescents’ perspectives and leadership should be institutionalized and actively supported in the design, implementation, and evaluation of health programs. Equity must guide all programming stages, ensuring no adolescent is left behind, with attention to age, sex, disability, and vulnerability. Sustainability of adolescent health programs requires shifting funding responsibility toward domestic resources. Advocacy based on investment cases for adolescent health priorities can help integrate these needs into national strategies, investment plans, and budgets. A logical framework for programming, as outlined in the AA-HA. guidance, links program goals, objectives, interventions, and strategies, ensuring a systematic response to adolescent health and well-being. This framework emphasizes the interconnectedness of well-being domains, such as health, education, and employability, and highlights the importance of addressing protective and risk factors across these domains. For example, addressing adolescent malnutrition requires considering macro-level policies, education, life skills, and empowerment to make healthy lifestyle choices.
